topic: Discovery stories / peptides your body makes: bradykinin, the peptide hiding in your blood that snake venom revealed. 1948-49 Rocha e Silva, Beraldo & Rosenfeld (São Paulo) found that Bothrops jararaca venom (or trypsin) acting on plasma globulin released a hypotensive, smooth-muscle-stimulating factor (Am J Physiol 1949;156:261); it caused a slow, delayed contraction of guinea pig ileum, hence brady (slow) + kinin (movement) (Motta & Tersariol, Front Physiol 2017; Graeff et al., Acta Neuropsychiatr 2024); 9 amino acids Arg-Pro-Pro-Gly-Phe-Ser-Pro-Phe-Arg released from high-molecular-weight kininogen by plasma kallikrein; causes vasodilation, increased microvessel permeability, edema and pain (Motta 2017); ACE (kininase II) and other enzymes inactivate it, circulating lifespan only a few seconds (Rex et al., Mol Biol Rep 2022)

cards.html:
Plate No. 1 · Brazil, 1948

Snake venom revealed a peptide hiding in your blood.

The experiment

São Paulo, 1948.

Three scientists mixed jararaca snake venom with blood plasma. Something new appeared.

The name

It made gut muscle contract slowly.

brady= slow
kinin= movement

Bradykinin.

The twist

It was never in the venom.

It sits locked inside a bigger blood protein, kininogen. Your enzyme kallikrein cuts it free. The venom made the same cut.

Field notes

9

amino acids. Once free, it:

1Widens blood vessels
2Makes them leaky, so tissue swells
3Switches on pain

Lifespan

Gone in seconds.

Enzymes in your blood, like ACE, chop it up almost as soon as it is made.

End of entry

Save this for your pharmacology exam.
